title: Dynamic sperm proteome remodelling during epididymal maturation in a marsupial, Macropus giganteus
projectDescription: While assisted reproductive technologies (ARTs) are widely used in domestic animals, successful implementation of ARTs to conserve wildlife species remains challenging. In macropods, crucial aspects of fundamental reproductive biology, including changes induced by epididymal maturation, remain unknown, limiting the development of ARTs. In this context we performed a proteomic analysis of spermatozoa from the caput, corpus, and cauda epididymis of Eastern Grey Kangaroos (n = 6) to profile changes over epididymal maturation. Samples prepared by FASP digestion were analysed by LC-MS/MS with SWATH acquisition. A total of 4,304 proteins were identified, with significant overlap across epididymal regions. Highly abundant proteins in common across caput, corpus and cauda spermatozoa had strong enrichment for tubulins and included 4 histone proteins. The most significant proteomic remodelling was observed in the corpus to cauda transition, late in epididymal transit (728 differentially abundant proteins). Overall proteomic changes across epididymal maturation (1,131 differentially abundant proteins) suggested a loss of sperm glycosidases and an increase in flagellar proteins, including tubulins and dyneins. These findings serve to highlight both consistencies with eutherian sperm epididymal maturation (e.g. bias towards protein loss over transit, transfer of proteins via extracellular vesicles) and elements which are likely unique to marsupials (e.g. reduced chromatin stability, potential use of β-oxidation as a major metabolic pathway). This critical information can now be leveraged to further develop ARTs in marsupials.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Isolation and Preparation of Spermatozoa  Spermatozoa were isolated and prepared individually for each male (n = 6). The left and right epididymides were isolated and cut into three sections (caput, corpus, and cauda) based on gross anatomical differences. Each section was rinsed in PBS to remove excess blood, minced in 2mL of tris-citrate buffer (300mM Tris, 95mM citrate, 28mM fructose, pH 7.4) containing 0.3% (w/v) bovine serum albumin (BSA) and incubated at 37°C for 15 minutes to allow sperm to ‘swim out’ from epididymal tissue. Following incubation, tissue was discarded and isolated sperm from the left and right epididymides were pooled within male and maintained at 37°C. Cauda epididymal samples were subjectively assessed for motility, and all samples met the minimum threshold of >60% motile (data not shown). Samples were then washed with tris-citrate buffer without BSA and centrifuged (1000xg, 5 min). The supernatant was discarded and the sperm pellet was stored at -80°C until further processing.  Preparation of Samples for Mass Spectrometry Lysis buffer (100µL; 10mM Tris, 2% (w/v) sodium dodecyl sulphate, 1x Sigma COmplete protease inhibitor, pH 8) was added to each frozen sperm pellet and incubated at room temperature for 1 hour. Samples were centrifuged (7500xg, 15 min) and supernatant protein concentration was determined by bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay (Pierce, Thermo Fisher Scientific, cat # 23225). A standardized load of 20µg total protein was prepared by filter-aided sample preparation (FASP). 30kDa MWCO spin filters (Amicon Ultra, Merck, cat # UFC5030) were washed with 8M urea in 50mM ammonium bicarbonate (UA) (13,000xg, 15 min). Lysate was added to prepared filters (13,000xg, 15 min) and washed twice with UA (13,000xg,15 min). Samples were reduced with 10mM dithiothreitol (30 min) and then alkylated with 50mM iodoacetamide (30 min in the dark). Samples were washed thoroughly with 8M urea, followed by 50mM ammonium bicarbonate (3x 13,000xg, 15 min each). Samples were digested with trypsin (1:50 trypsin:total protein, in 0.01% (w/v) ProteaseMax, Promega, cat # V5113, V2071) overnight at 37°C. Resulting peptides were eluted with 50mM ammonium bicarbonate. The flow-through was dried by vacuum centrifuge and resuspended in 0.5% (v/v) formic acid (FA). A final cleanup was performed with C18 ziptips (~5µg binding capacity, Millipore, cat # ZTC18S). Peptides were eluted with 0.1% (v/v) FA, 80% (v/v) acetonitrile, dried by vacuum centrifuge and resuspended in 20µl 0.1% (v/v) FA prior to injection. LC-MS/MS and SWATH Acquisition All biological replicates were analysed individually by LC-MS/MS. Samples were separated using reversed-phase chromatography on a Waters M-Class UPLC system. Samples were loaded onto a Waters NanoEase HSS T3 column (100 A, 1.8 um, 300 um x 150 mm). Chromatography was performed at 5µL/min and column set at 40°C, with LC conditions as follows: 0 – 0.5 min = 3% B, 0.5- 30.5 min = 3-30%, 30.5-34.5 min = 30-60% 34.5-36.5 60- 97%, held at 97% for 4 min followed by re-equilibration for 4 min. Pump A = 0.1% (v/v) FA in water, and pump B = 0.1% (v/v) FA in acetonitrile. Eluted peptides were directly analysed on a ZenoTof 7600 instrument (ABSciex) using an OptiFlow Micro/MicroCal source. Curtain gas = 35 psi, CAD gas = 7, Gas 1 = 20 psi, Gas 2 = 15 psi, source temp = 150°C, spray voltage = 5000 V, DP = 80, CE = 10. For Zeno-SWATH acquisitions, MS TOF scan across 400-1500 m/z was performed (0.1 sec). For MS2, variable windows spanning 399.5 m/z – 750.5 m/z were chosen for fragmentation (0.013 sec) with fragment data acquired across 140 – 1750 m/z with Zeno pulsing on, with threshold set to 100000 cps. Dynamic collision energy was used. A bovine serum albumin standard was employed for quality control between runs.
dataProcessingProtocol: Protein identification and quantification were performed using DIA-NN (Demichev et al., 2020, v1.9.2). An in silico ion spectral library was generated using two Uniprot FASTA files for the closely related Koala (Phascolarctos cinereus) and Wombat (Vombatus unsinus) (downloaded January 2025), with default search parameters.  The DIA-NN output report was reformatted using the R package MSstats_labelfree_preprocessing and subsequently the R package MSstats (Choi et al. 2014) was used to perform filtering and statistical analysis of protein abundance in R Studio (v 2021.09.0).
